implementation_notes: Python's encapsulation unit is the module: its namespace is private by construction, names starting with `_` are understood as internal, `__all__` declares what the module offers, and a class in that module needs to name no other model class. A standalone class is therefore an ordinary class with `_`-prefixed module-level helpers, `__slots__` to close the instance namespace, and operations returning the class's own type; the classic 'private members' structure is replaced by module privacy plus naming convention. Python enforces none of it, so a test that imports the class alone is the real boundary check. Since 3.7 the standard library supplies the value-carrier form; before that, hand-written `__eq__`/`__hash__` was the only option.
pitfalls: Privacy is a convention: `_name` is only a hint and `__name` merely name-mangles, so nothing stops a caller from reading or writing internals - the boundary has to be defended in review and by tests.
Circular imports are fatal at import time: a standalone module that imports another model module for one helper turns coupling into a startup error.
`from module import *` honours `__all__`, but direct attribute access does not, so the public surface is a declaration rather than an enforced contract.
`__slots__` blocks new attributes on instances but not subclasses (unless they also declare slots), and it prevents `__dict__`-based tricks some frameworks rely on.

variants.name: Frozen dataclass as the standalone value
variants.implementation_notes: Since 3.7 `@dataclass(frozen=True)` writes the carrier for you: the annotated fields declare the state, and `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__` and - because `frozen=True` with `eq=True` - `__hash__` are generated, with `__post_init__` holding validation and `dataclasses.replace` as the functional update. Adding `slots=True` (3.10+) or an explicit `__slots__` closes the instance namespace so no ad-hoc attribute can appear, which keeps the type's meaning exactly its declaration. This is the idiomatic modern form of a standalone value in Python; the hand-written class stays better when the type has behaviour beyond its data, needs custom equality, or must run on Python < 3.7.
pitfalls: `frozen=True` freezes the reference, not the contents: a list or dict field is still mutable, and the generated `__hash__` then hashes a mutable object.
`dataclasses.replace` and `copy` are shallow: nested values are shared with the copy, so changing them changes the original.
Inheritance plus defaulted fields is fragile - a non-default field after a defaulted one raises at class creation - so subclassing dataclasses with defaults needs `kw_only=True` fields.
Equality compares class and all fields: adding a field later changes the hash of values already used as dictionary keys or set members.
